reviews.title: JIRA - an ALM Architect's perspective
reviews.text: Versatile to its core, JIRA allows administrators the ability to create customized issue types (building data entry forms) and workflow for virtually any kind of business artifact within any IT domain: ALM (software defect tracking), ITSM (service desk management), PPM (agile portfolio management), etc. An Enterprise Application Administrator's playground of fun, JIRA can (and must) be customized to work for project teams and end-users. Consider three pitfalls when adopting JIRA - two pertaining to administration teams and one pertaining to end-users. Admin Pitfall #1: while JIRA does in fact allow administrators the ability to build customized issue types, workflows and artifacts, JIRA's core functionality isn't designed or delivered to support all of the customized artifacts that end up being created. And so, a growing JIRA instance ends up becoming a performance nightmare of additional plugins for extended functionality. Defined administration standards and practices can help control and manage customization. Otherwise, maintenance, support levels and cost increase with each customization. Admin Pitfall #2: The JIRA application is designed around the concept of reusing fields across multiple projects. Administrators end up managing a collection of customized fields for project reuse. And so, from this concept, extends JIRA's poor MVC design - presenting UX confusion and introducing inconsistencies at each level of architecture (especially in the GUI). Rather than JIRA itself managing the relationships and associations between fields within a project's schema (as other enterprise applications do), JIRA decouples these relationships and associations from the schema and puts this responsibility on the administrator. When field attributes and properties change, administrators are now "managing" DueDate, DueDate2, DueDate3, DueDate4, etc. End-User Pitfall: Compared to other polished enterprise software packages, JIRA's GUI is confusing and is not intuitive. reviews.title: Platform actively misused for spam and phishing — support ignores the real problem
reviews.text: I have never been an Atlassian customer, yet I regularly receive spam, phishing attempts, and scam messages delivered via Atlassian's own notification system. Criminals create Jira or Confluence accounts, add arbitrary email addresses to projects, and Atlassian's infrastructure then delivers the messages — from a trusted domain that bypasses standard spam filters. This is a well-documented abuse vector. What makes this worse: Atlassian's abuse process does not address the actual problem. When I contacted support, instead of blacklisting my addresses from ever being added to a project, they processed an account deletion request I never made. The core issue — that anyone can weaponize their platform to reach people who never consented — was completely ignored. There is a third concern that Atlassian users may not think about: companies routinely paste passwords, API keys, and other sensitive data into Jira tickets. Atlassian then sends these out as plaintext email notifications to every watcher — including people who were added without their knowledge. This is a serious security and data protection issue. The fix is straightforward: make notifications strictly opt-in. Nobody should receive Atlassian emails unless they explicitly signed up. Until that changes, the platform remains a convenient tool for anyone wanting to reach people who have no relationship with Atlassian whatsoever.
